The answer is complex, but the short of it is because most of the people voting for progressive or socialist candidates are first or second generation immigrants. Granting amnesty to illegal immigrants buys up a huge future voting pool when either those granted amnesty become citizens, or they have children that are born natural citizens.

It also helps that the "we have enough to take care of everybody" mentality of progressives and socialists does fall in line with the concept that "everybody that comes to us for help should be helped." Not everyone will agree, of course, but it's not like the two concepts are ideologically exclusive.

Leaving aside anything unique to the US, I'm a social democrat, ie a socialist. I'm also politically active. I have met and talked to a lot of like minded people both for and against a generous immigration policy (here in Sweden). First you have to realize that socialism is about what we'd like to see society be like, and understand that you can share a goal with someone without agreeing on how to get there. Socialists in favour of generous immigration policies generally justify it, quite sincerely, by saying that they want to improve as many lives as possible as much as possible, and as immigrants are almost exclusively people who left their home to seek a better life for themselves or their family, helping them often results in more utility/happiness per dollar spent than if you'd sealed your borders and just helped the people who were already here and on their feet. Socialists not in favour of much immigration typically justify it by saying that per dollar spent, we can help more people if they remain in their home country than if we wait for them to come here, where food and housing is much more expensive. The end goal in each case is a world where anyone can expect a good quality of life, no matter where they are from, but arrived at by different paths. In reality we see a bit of both; helping people who come here, but also giving aid to less well to do states so they can improve things for their population at large.

Protecting the rights of illegal immigrants will not appeal to the latter kind of socialist, but it will to the former, who see them as equals who should be treated like citizens, or as close to it as feasible. Almost everyone agrees that opening the flood gates fully is not realistic, and that improvements have to be gradual.

I like Bernie, but I'm not an expert on US politics,, so I won't claim to speak on behalf of him or his American supporters.

Many socialists are not nationalists, meaning they do not believe that a nation should prioritize their own citizens over those of other countries. Those who share this view are more in line with classical Marxism, which calls for a global workers' revolution not limited to any one country.

In other words, there are two dramatically different brands of socialists: national socialists, who support policies that benefit the people (especially the working classes) within their own country, and international socialists, who support policies (such as open borders) that benefit the working classes of the entire world, viewing nationality as subordinate to class.

Of course, one can make the argument that open borders don't actually benefit anyone, least of all the global working classes, but it's more a disagreement of ideals than of practicality.
